stocktake_row.File: Blanco‐Sacristán et al. - 2022 - Mangrove distribution and afforestation potential in the Red Sea.pdf
stocktake_row.Input_Variables: AMT (WorldClim); MDRM (WorldClim); IBIO (WorldClim); TS (WorldClim); MTWM (WorldClim); MTCM (WorldClim); TARBIO (WorldClim); MTWeQ (WorldClim); MTDQ (WorldClim); MTWaQ (WorldClim); MTCQ (WorldClim); AP (WorldClim); PWM (WorldClim); PDM (WorldClim); PS (WorldClim); PWeQ (WorldClim); PDQ (WorldClim); PWaQ (WorldClim); PCQ (WorldClim); Elevation (ALOS DSM); SSTmean (NASA MODIS-Aqua Level-3); SSTmin (NASA MODIS-Aqua Level-3); SSTmax (NASA MODIS-Aqua Level-3); SSTrange (NASA MODIS-Aqua Level-3); SSS (Bio-Oracle); PARmean (Bio-Oracle); PARmax (Bio-Oracle); pH (Bio-Oracle); Clay (OpenLandMap); Bulk (OpenLandMap); Texture (OpenLandMap); Sand (OpenLandMap)
stocktake_row.Spatial_Method: MaxEnt presence-only species distribution modeling using environmental and soil variables to identify suitable mangrove restoration/afforestation areas; CART-based supervised classification of Sentinel-2 imagery (NDVI) to map current mangrove extent and delineate priority areas.
stocktake_row.Method_Validation: Cross-validation (10 replicates) with MaxEnt (75% training, 25% testing) and ROC/AUC evaluation; CART classification validation via confusion matrices (user, producer, overall accuracies) with 20 splits; cross-sensor validation by comparing Sentinel-2 mangrove maps with Landsat 8 results; validation by comparison with existing mangrove extent maps from previous studies.
stocktake_row.Tool: MaxEnt (Phillips et al., 2004) ; CART (Breiman et al., 1984)
stocktake_row.Tool_Source: MaxEnt : Used to map the potential distribution of Red Sea mangroves and identify afforestation sites by modeling presence-only mangrove occurrences (5000 centroids) against a 32-variable environmental/soil dataset with 10,000 background points, via the dismo MaxEnt implementation in R, producing a 0–1 suitability map (AUC = 0.86) and enabling estimation of current and potential carbon sequestration (with 10-fold cross-validation). ; CART : Used to map current mangrove extent from Sentinel-2 imagery by applying a Classification and Regression Tree using NDVI and eight Sentinel-2 bands at 10 m, with 420 points per class across 20 random splits, achieving high accuracies (~97.6% overall) and producing high-resolution mangrove extent maps (also contrasted with Landsat‑8 results).
stocktake_row.Output: Potential mangrove afforestation suitability map (occurrence probability >0.5; classes: low/medium/high)
stocktake_row.Narrative: The NbS addressed were mangrove afforestation/restoration along the Red Sea for climate mitigation and coastal protection. Main inputs included Sentinel-2 imagery at 10 m for current mangroves (≈98% accuracy) and NDVI, plus a 32-variable bioclimatic/soil dataset from WorldClim, ALOS DSM, NASA MODIS SST, Bio-Oracle, and OpenLandMap; 5,000 presence centroids and 10,000 background points. Spatial method: current extent mapped with CART at 10 m; potential distribution modeled with MaxEnt (75/25 train/test; 10-fold CV; AUC 0.86) using the 32 variables after removing non-contributors and retaining non-collinear pairs (r<0.8). The MaxEnt output (>0.5) was resampled to 10 m to yield 410.9 km2 potential and 175.3 km2 current mangroves (S2), with per-country totals. Validation showed mangrove-class accuracy ≈98% (S2) and overall 97.6%; soil variables explained ≈91% of potential distribution. Outputs include 10 m maps; carbon sequestration estimates: current 1034 ± 181 Mg C yr−1 and potential 2424 ± 423 Mg C yr−1; no economic analysis. Geographic scope: Red Sea region. Climate risk addressed via carbon sequestration; economic considerations were not analyzed.
stocktake_row.Scalability_A_Justification: The spatial analysis (MaxEnt modeling of mangrove distribution) was applied across the Red Sea region, covering multiple bordering countries (Djibouti, Egypt, Eritrea, Saudi Arabia, Sudan, Yemen) with country-level results, i.e., a multi-country regional scope.
stocktake_row.Scalability_B_Justification: Reasoning: The study presents a standard, modular workflow—CART-based mangrove mapping from Sentinel-2 data in GEE and a MaxEnt niche model using a fixed set of global environmental predictors with documented parameters—that can be replicated in other regions with region-specific training data, making it highly transferable.
stocktake_row.Scalability_C_Justification: Reasoning: The study relies largely on globally available, open datasets (Sentinel-2 imagery via Google Earth Engine; WorldClim bioclimatic layers; ALOS DSM; Bio-Oracle marine/soil layers; OpenLandMap soil properties; global SST/SSS/PAR/pH data) with only a localized training/validation set (420 points per class) and presence data tied to the Red Sea region; these local inputs could be substituted with other open regional data to replicate elsewhere.
stocktake_row.oa_title: Mangrove distribution and afforestation potential in the Red Sea

stocktake_row.File: Sahana et al. - 2022 - Assessment of suitable habitat of mangrove species for prioritizing restoration in coastal ecosystem.pdf
stocktake_row.NbS_Subpractice: ecological mangrove restoration (EMR); community-based restoration approaches; ecological engineering; ecosystem design
stocktake_row.Input_Variables: Elevation (Appendix 1); Slope (Appendix 1); Curvature (Appendix 1); Geomorphology (Appendix 1); TWI (Appendix 1); SPI (Appendix 1); NDVI (Appendix 2B); Level of flood inundation (Appendix 1); Mean tidal range (Appendix 1); Storm surge height (Appendix 1); NDMI (Appendix 1); Rate of erosion/accretion (Appendix 1); Water surface temperature (Appendix 1); Water salinity (Appendix 1); pH value (Appendix 1); Distance from water (Appendix 1); Drainage density (Appendix 1); NDWI (Appendix 2C); Soil texture (Appendix 2D); Soil salinity index (Appendix 2D); Soil fertility index (Appendix 2D); Sediment yield factor (Appendix 2D); Electronic conductivity (Appendix 2D); Vegetation soil salinity index (VSSI) (Appendix 2D); BIO1 (WorldClim); BIO2 (WorldClim); BIO3 (WorldClim); BIO4 (WorldClim); BIO12 (WorldClim); BIO15 (WorldClim); Distance from road (Appendix 2F); Road density (Appendix 2F); Distance from Settlement (Appendix 2F); Population density (Appendix 2F); Distance from crop field (Appendix 2F); Embankment density (Appendix 2F)
stocktake_row.Spatial_Method: Ensemble habitat suitability modeling using ten machine-learning models in biomod2 to produce species-specific suitability maps; niche overlap analysis (Modified Hellinger I and Schoener’s D) using raster overlay in ArcGIS; grid-based restoration prioritization across 1 km grids using PCA-derived ranking and multi-criteria indicator scoring (positive/negative) to identify priority grids.
stocktake_row.Method_Validation: 80/20 train–test split for model validation (and 75/25 intrinsic validation within models); intrinsic validation metrics (Cohen’s Kappa, TSS, ROC); extrinsic validation with Boyce Index on held‑out data (20%) to select models for the ensemble; field verification/ground-truthing of degraded areas and GPS-verified occurrence data; niche overlap analysis with PCA-based validation of species niches; independent validation dataset via BI; validation of input layers with Landsat-based LULC accuracy (confusion matrix and kappa for 1975 and 2020).
stocktake_row.Tool_Source: biomod2 (CRAN) : Used to run an ensemble of 10 species distribution models for 18 mangrove species, generating final habitat suitability maps via a weighted-mean ensemble and evaluating models with Kappa, TSS, ROC and Boyce index before selecting the ensemble for restoration-prioritization mapping; MAXENT (Phillips et al., 2006 Ecography) : One of the ten machine-learning algorithms included in the biomod2 ensemble used to model habitat suitability/distribution of mangrove species from occurrence data and environmental predictors.
stocktake_row.Output: Ensemble habitat suitability map for 18 mangrove species (classes: highly suitable; moderately suitable; slightly suitable; not suitable); Grid-based restoration priority map for Sundarban Biosphere Reserve (1‑km grids; 1,203 prioritized grids; 8 priority categories); Species niche‑overlap (grid‑based spatial similarity/dissimilarity)
stocktake_row.Climate_Barrier: Yes: The study treats erosion hazard and rainfall-driven water availability as risks that limit peanut and sengon suitability and performance, demonstrated by a risk-screening land-suitability matching approach that classifies land units and outputs sub-classes explicitly constrained by “erosion hazard” and “water availability.”
stocktake_row.Narrative: Nature-based solution targeted mangrove restoration in the Sundarbans Biosphere Reserve, India, by assessing habitat suitability for 18 mangrove species with an ensemble of 10 ML models in biomod2. The inputs encompassed 36 variables spanning topography, bioclimatic layers, environmental/water metrics, soil attributes and disturbance indicators, derived from Landsat land-cover maps (1975 MSS, 2020 OLI) and 1 km grid coverage over 5609 cells; occurrence data from GBIF, literature and 950 field samples (1560 after rarefaction) plus Landsat land-cover data. Ten models were validated with an 80/20 split; ensemble via weighted mean; models with >0.75 performance used; Boyce index confirmed ensemble (avg ROC/TSS/KAPPA ≈0.90). Outputs are four-class habitat maps at 1 km, with 36.6% highly suitable and 1203 restoration-priority grids in eight categories across SBR. Climate risk and economic factors were included via bioclimatic and disturbance variables.
stocktake_row.Scalability_A_Justification: The spatial analysis (habitat suitability modeling and restoration prioritization) was applied entirely within the Sundarban Biosphere Reserve in India, i.e., a single sub-national area
stocktake_row.Scalability_B_Justification: Reasoning: The study presents a broadly standard, reproducible workflow—ensemble species distribution modeling with biomod2, PCA-based variable reduction, and a grid-based restoration prioritization using general indicators—that can be applied elsewhere with regional data, and the authors themselves suggest its applicability to other regions.
stocktake_row.Scalability_C_Justification: Key data sources include GBIF-derived mangrove species occurrences plus local field surveys, Landsat-based land-use/land-cover change (1975 and 2020), WorldClim bioclimatic layers, global DEM/topographic derivatives (e.g., TWI, SPI), NDVI, SoilGrids soil variables, and disturbance proxies (road/population/embankments) from open global datasets; since these inputs are largely open-access global datasets, the approach is highly generalizable to other regions with equivalent data, though region-specific occurrence data and local species lists would be needed.
stocktake_row.oa_title: Assessment of suitable habitat of mangrove species for prioritizing restoration in coastal ecosystem of Sundarban Biosphere Reserve, India

stocktake_row.File: Hu et al. - 2020 - Mapping the potential of mangrove forest restoration based on species distribution models A case st.pdf
stocktake_row.Input_Variables: bio_01 (WorldClim); bio_02 (WorldClim); bio_03 (WorldClim); bio_04 (WorldClim); bio_05 (WorldClim); bio_06 (WorldClim); bio_07 (WorldClim); bio_08 (WorldClim); bio_09 (WorldClim); bio_10 (WorldClim); bio_11 (WorldClim); bio_12 (WorldClim); bio_13 (WorldClim); bio_14 (WorldClim); bio_15 (WorldClim); bio_16 (WorldClim); bio_17 (WorldClim); bio_18 (WorldClim); bio_19 (WorldClim); Etopo1 (NOAA); LD (Geomorphometric and Gradient Metrics Toolbox); CTI (Geomorphometric and Gradient Metrics Toolbox); sbdare (not specified); sst1 (NASA MODIS-Aqua Level-3); sst2 (NASA MODIS-Aqua Level-3); sst3 (NASA MODIS-Aqua Level-3); sst4 (NASA MODIS-Aqua Level-3); sst5 (NASA MODIS-Aqua Level-3); sst6 (NASA MODIS-Aqua Level-3); sst7 (NASA MODIS-Aqua Level-3)
stocktake_row.Spatial_Method: MaxEnt presence-only SDM; GARP presence-only SDM; then constrain predicted suitability with land-use/land-cover data and compute a restoration potential index (RPI = Si × Ti) to identify restorable/priority areas.
stocktake_row.Method_Validation: Train-test split validation with AUC/ROC (75% training, 25% testing); comparison with 361 existing mangrove restoration projects to assess alignment; direct model comparison between GARP and MaxEnt (MaxEnt preferred); expert validation of land-use/land-cover transfer coefficients via a questionnaire of 10 experts.
stocktake_row.Tool: MaxEnt (Phillips et al., 2006) ; OpenModeller Desktop 1.5.1 (Munoz et al., 2011)
stocktake_row.Tool_Source: MaxEnt : Used to model mangrove habitat suitability and potential distribution using presence-only data, producing a probability-of-occurrence map (0–1), evaluating with AUC, and providing the final, more accurate distribution/restoration-potential predictions (e.g., about 16,800 ha restorable area) that best matched known mangrove patterns; OpenModeller Desktop 1.5.1 : Used to run the GARP model (genetic algorithm for rule-set prediction) for mangroves on presence-only data, producing multiple rule-based binary suitability outputs that were averaged and compared with MaxEnt outputs for validation and restoration-potential mapping.
stocktake_row.Output: Mangrove habitat suitability map (MaxEnt) [high/medium/low]; Restoration Potential Index (RPI) map of potentially restorable areas (MaxEnt; RPI 0–1; restorable >0.5)
stocktake_row.Geographic_Scope: National: China; Sub-national: Zhejiang; Fujian; Guangdong; Guangxi; Hainan
stocktake_row.Narrative: NbS addressed: mangrove restoration as a nature‑based solution for coastal protection and ecosystem services. Main inputs: 3839 mangrove occurrence points (remote sensing and on‑site surveys); 1 km environmental data including bioclimatic variables, SST metrics, elevation, CTI, and substrate from WorldClim, NASA MODIS‑Aqua, and ETOPO1; 2018 land‑use/land‑cover from RESDC; ESRI imagery for patch interpretation. Spatial method and combination: two presence‑only SDMs, GARP and MaxEnt; 75% of data used for training and 25% for testing; MaxEnt AUC 0.953 and GARP 0.882; restoration potential index (RPI) computed as RPI = S_i × T_i using LULC‑based transfer coefficients; grids with RPI > 0.5 designated restorable and overlaid with 361 restoration projects. Validation and results: MaxEnt outperformed GARP; northern limit around 28°27′–28°35′ N; nationwide restorable areas 16,800 ha (MaxEnt) versus 420,800 ha (GARP) after excluding extant mangroves; about 75% of potential areas lost to land use. Outputs and resolution: 1 km RPI map across Zhejiang, Fujian, Guangdong, Guangxi, and Hainan. Geographic scope: coastal mainland China (18°10′–29°30′ N). Climate predictors included; economic considerations via LULC transfer coefficients; no explicit climate‑risk or cost analysis.
stocktake_row.Scalability_A_Justification: The spatial analysis (SDMs for mangrove restoration potential) was applied across the coastal region of mainland China, covering five provinces (Zhejiang, Fujian, Guangdong, Guangxi, and Hainan), i.e., a national-scale analysis for China.
stocktake_row.Scalability_B_Justification: The approach uses a generalizable workflow (presence-only SDMs with global climate/topographic predictors) to map habitat suitability and then integrates a land-use transfer-coefficient step to estimate restorable potential, which could be applied elsewhere with global data. However, the transfer coefficients and threshold-based decisions for restorable areas are locally defined (expert-based LULC transfer), so substantial local adaptation is required, preventing full transfer without effort
stocktake_row.Scalability_C_Justification: Key data sources include globally accessible climate (WorldClim at ~1 km), sea surface temperature (MODIS), and elevation (ETOPO1); however, the land-use/land-cover data are a China-specific 1-km RESDC dataset (with transfer coefficients tailored to Chinese coastal LULC types) and mangrove occurrences come from Chinese patches plus on-site validation. Because the core climate/elevation/SST inputs are global/open but the LULC, transfer coefficients, and occurrence data are region-specific (with local validation), the approach is MIXED in generalizability
stocktake_row.oa_title: Mapping the potential of mangrove forest restoration based on species distribution models: A case study in China

stocktake_row.File: Borges et al. - 2017 - Systematic Planning and Ecosystem-Based Management as Strategies to Reconcile Mangrove Conservation.pdf
stocktake_row.Input_Variables: Mangrove distribution (Giri et al., 2011); Protected areas (IUCN UNEP-WCMC, 2017); Site-specific climate change impacts (Godoy and Lacerda, 2015); Beach erosion (Ward et al., 2016); Port activities (Cunha, 2006; Ferreira and Lacerda, 2016a); Urbanization (Ferreira and Lacerda, 2016a); Geomorphological conditions (Souza Filho and Paradella, 2002); Hydrographic conditions (Souza Filho and Paradella, 2002); Vegetation patterns (Menezes et al., 2008); CBERS imagery (Santos et al., 2014); SPOT imagery (Santos et al., 2014); Landsat TM (Souza Filho and Paradella, 2002); RADARSAT-1 (Souza Filho and Paradella, 2002)
stocktake_row.Spatial_Method: No explicit spatial analysis method is described; it advocates GIS-based information within a systematic conservation planning framework and notes tools such as Marxan and InVEST as potential approaches.
stocktake_row.Tool: InVEST (Guerry et al., 2012) ; Marxan (Ball et al., 2009)
stocktake_row.Tool_Source: InVEST : Not used in this study; cited as a potential modeling/decision-support tool to inform systematic planning and ecosystem-based mangrove management. ; Marxan : Not used in this study; cited as a potential decision-support tool for spatial conservation prioritization in mangrove planning.
stocktake_row.Output: Mangrove distribution and protection-level map by macro-unit [North, Northeast, East, Southeast; protection classes: strictly protected, sustainable-use, forest-component-only, unknown]
stocktake_row.Narrative: NbS addressed: systematic planning and ecosystem-based mangrove management, treating mangroves as an integrated social–ecological system with multi-scale spatial planning and GIS synthesis to balance conservation and use. Main inputs and data sources: mangrove extent (Giri et al. 2011); protected areas (IUCN/UNEP-WCMC 2017); a four-macro-unit framework (North, Northeast, East, Southeast) informed by Knoppers (1999) and Ferreira & Lacerda (2016a,b); climate change and drivers (Godoy & Lacerda 2015; Ward 2016); geomorphology/hydrography (Souza Filho & Paradella 2002; Menezes 2008); satellite imagery (Landsat/CBERS/SPOT) and MADAM Bragança data. Spatial method and data fusion: national four-macro-unit classification based on social–ecological and climatic traits, with GIS overlays of distribution, protection, drivers and uses to inform policy. Validation: not reported. Key results: the four macro-units with distinct protection levels; North 66% sustainable-use, 15% strictly protected; Northeast ~66% unprotected; East large protected in sustainable-use areas, ~0.5% strictly protected; Southeast >20% strictly protected, ~33% inside environmental protected areas. Outputs: macro-unit map (Figure 1) and Table 1 at national scale; Bragança highlighted (6,516 km2, 4.3% of mangroves, >80% of Brazilian mangroves). Climate risk and economic considerations included via projections and shrimp/salt/fisheries uses.
stocktake_row.Scalability_A_Justification: The spatial approach is applied nationally across Brazil, using national-scale GIS data to define four macro-units that span the entire Brazilian coast; thus, the largest scale demonstrated is country-wide.
stocktake_row.Scalability_B_Justification: The paper offers a general GIS-based planning framework (multi-scale, standardized data, social-ecological integration) that could be adapted elsewhere, but its Brazil-specific macro-units and governance context would require regional redefinition and local weight calibration
stocktake_row.Scalability_C_Justification: Key data sources cited as inputs are the global mangrove distribution map (Giri et al. 2011) and global protected area data (WDPA from IUCN/UNEP-WCMC, 2017), both open and widely used; the approach also hinges on standard GIS data (e.g., global DEMs/coastlines) and climate/biophysical context from literature, not on region-specific private datasets, making the data requirements broadly replicable in other regions with equivalent global layers. This suggests high generalizability (mainly global/open-input data) for replication elsewhere
stocktake_row.oa_title: Systematic Planning and Ecosystem-Based Management as Strategies to Reconcile Mangrove Conservation with Resource Use

stocktake_row.File: Aduana-Alcantara et al. - 2023 - Mangrove Land Suitability Assessment Using Weighted Linear Combination A Case Study of La Union Pro.pdf
stocktake_row.Input_Variables: Elevation (ASTER Global Digital Elevation Map); Slope (ASTER Global Digital Elevation Map); Air Temperature (Global Solar Atlas); Precipitation (WorldClim)
stocktake_row.Spatial_Method: GIS-based multicriteria analysis using Weighted Linear Combination (WLC) in ArcMap, integrating raster layers of elevation, slope, precipitation, and air temperature with equal weights to produce mangrove suitability classes.
stocktake_row.Output: Mangrove land suitability map for La Union Province (classes: unsuitable, marginally suitable, moderately suitable, highly suitable)
stocktake_row.Geographic_Scope: Sub-national: La Union Province;Aringay;Bangar;Sto. Tomas;City of San Fernando;Agoo;Balaoan;Bauang National: Philippines;Vietnam;Indonesia;Australia;Papua New Guinea;Malaysia;Iran;Saudi Arabia
stocktake_row.Narrative: The NbS addressed were mangrove rehabilitation and reforestation along La Union Province coastline. The main inputs were elevation and slope from the ASTER GDEM, and bioclimatic factors—air temperature from the Global Solar Atlas and precipitation from WorldClim—at 30-arc second resolution; La Union spans about 1,497 km2. The spatial method used was a GIS-based Weighted Linear Combination (WLC) in ArcMap, combining layers with S = sum Wi Xi, where Xi is the class score and Wi the weight; weights were assumed equal. Validation: no field validation was described; ground truthing was emphasized. Key results identified four suitable sites along the coast within Bangar, San Fernando, Aringay, and Sto. Tomas; Agoo, Balaoan, and Bauang were not reflected due to data resolution. Outputs included a mangrove land suitability map (30 s) and four sites. Geographic scope: provincial scale, La Union, Philippines. Climate risk was included via temperature and precipitation; economic factors were not.
stocktake_row.Scalability_A_Justification: The WLC GIS analysis was applied to the La Union Province coastline in the Philippines, i.e., a sub-national (provincial) area
stocktake_row.Scalability_B_Justification: The method is a generic GIS-based Weighted Linear Combination (WLC) multicriteria analysis using a simple, globally parameterized formula (S = sum Wi Xi) with equal weights and globally available covariates, which can be applied in other regions with minimal adaptation (local weights or extra criteria can be added if desired)
stocktake_row.Scalability_C_Justification: Reasoning: The input suite is dominated by globally available open datasets—ASTER GDEM for elevation, WorldClim for precipitation, and the Global Solar Atlas for temperature—all at around 30-arc-second resolution, with minimal reliance on region-specific proprietary data aside from basic administrative context; this supports straightforward replication in other regions using the same/global data.
stocktake_row.oa_title: Mangrove Land Suitability Assessment Using Weighted Linear Combination: A Case Study of La Union Province Coastline, Philippines
stocktake_row.journal_name: Journal of Sustainability and Environmental Management

stocktake_row.File: Al‐Huqail et al. - 2024 - An ML-Based Ensemble Approach for the Precision Classification of Mangroves, Trend Analysis, and Pri.pdf
stocktake_row.Input_Variables: NDVI (Landsat 8 OLI 2023; Landsat Collection 1 Tier 1); NDWI (Landsat 8 OLI 2023; Landsat Collection 1 Tier 1); LST (Landsat 5-8 thermal bands; Landsat Collection 1 Tier 1); τNDVI (Kendall tau-b; Landsat 5-8 time series 1991–2023); τNDWI (Kendall tau-b; Landsat 5-8 time series 1991–2023); τLST (Kendall tau-b; Landsat 5-8 time series 1991–2023)
stocktake_row.Spatial_Method: Generalized additive model (GAM) using NDVI, LST, NDWI and their Kendall tau-b trends to derive a normalized suitability score for mangrove plantation; Moran’s I analysis to assess spatial clustering of the suitability.
stocktake_row.Method_Validation: Independent accuracy assessment using independent test samples with confusion matrix metrics (OA, producer and user accuracy, KC); 60/40 train–validation split for ML mangrove classification with stratified random sampling; 10-fold cross-validation for GAM to assess robustness; Visual validation with high‑resolution Google Earth imagery and NDVI overlay; Comparison with the Global Mangrove Watch (GMW) dataset; Moran’s I analysis to assess spatial clustering of the suitability.
stocktake_row.Tool: Google Earth Engine (Landsat Collections in Earth Engine; https://developers.google.com/earth-engine/datasets/catalog/landsat) ; mgcv (CRAN; https://cran.r-project.org/package=mgcv) ; XGBoost (GitHub; https://github.com/dmlc/xgboost) ; Asir (GitHub; https://github.com/zubairgis/Asir.git)
stocktake_row.Tool_Source: Google Earth Engine: Used to access, process, and analyze Landsat data (Landsat Collection 1 Tier 1) for 1991–2023 and 2023, generating annual cloud-free median composites, applying QA-based masking and atmospheric correction, computing spectral indices, and supporting the mangrove classification workflow. ; mgcv: Used in R to fit a generalized additive model (GAM) for mangrove plantation suitability, using cubic-spline smooth terms for NDVI, LST, NDWI and their Kendall tau-b trends, with cross-validation and diagnostics to assess model performance. ; XGBoost: One of the ensemble classifiers (RF, SVM, XGB) used to discriminate mangrove vs non-mangrove areas, with XGB achieving strong performance and undergoing hyperparameter tuning. ; Asir: A GitHub-hosted repository providing the mangrove data produced by the ML classifiers from this study, enabling data sharing/access.
stocktake_row.Output: Mangrove plantation suitability map (classes: not suitable; moderately suitable; highly suitable)
stocktake_row.Narrative: NbS addressed: mangrove conservation and priority reforestation to enhance coastal protection and resilience along the Asir coast, Saudi Arabia. Inputs and data sources included Landsat data (Landsat 8 OLI 2023; 1991–2023 Landsat 5–8), spectral indices (NDVI, NDWI, SR, GCVI) and LST, elevation from ASTER GDEM, 37,682 ML training/testing pixels (60/40), 399 reference points, Google Earth Engine, and Global Mangrove Watch for comparison. The spatial method and data fusion used an ensemble classification of mangrove vs non-mangrove with RF, SVM, and XGB and majority voting, coupled with NDVI/NDWI and elevation masking; outputs were at 30 m resolution, yielding mangrove area 14.69 km2 distributed across groups a–e (2.46, 4.48, 2.37, 4.55, 0.83 km2). A GAM-based reforestation suitability analysis integrated 2023 NDVI, LST, NDWI and their Kendall’s tau-b trends with weights (NDVI=3); adj R2=0.89 and R2=0.91, with 77% of Group e highly suitable. Validation used OA 91.3% and KC 0.83, plus a 10-fold CV and Moran’s I for clustering. Scope: Asir coast (≈200 km × 10 km). Climate variables included; no economic analysis.
stocktake_row.Scalability_A_Justification: The spatial analysis (mangrove classification, trend analysis, and GAM reforestation suitability) was applied specifically to the Asir coast region in Saudi Arabia (a sub-national/local area).
stocktake_row.Scalability_B_Justification: The method presents a standard, reproducible ML+trend+GAM framework using globally available Landsat data and open-source tools, which could be applied elsewhere, but requires region-specific training data and local calibration (e.g., model retraining, parameter/weight adjustments) to achieve similar performance; thus it is not fully universal without local adaptation.
stocktake_row.Scalability_C_Justification: Reasoning: The study primarily relies on globally available, open-access remote sensing data (Landsat 5–8 time series 1991–2023 and 2023 Landsat data; NDVI/NDWI/GCVI/SR indices; LST derived from Landsat; elevation from ASTER GDEM) accessed via Google Earth Engine, with a global mangrove reference (GMW) for comparison and only locally generated training/reference samples; thus the same workflow could be reproduced in other regions using equivalent global data. The few local elements (training and reference samples, site-specific GAM weighting) can be substituted with region-specific data, making the approach highly generalizable.
stocktake_row.oa_title: An ML-Based Ensemble Approach for the Precision Classification of Mangroves, Trend Analysis, and Priority Reforestation Areas in Asir, Saudi Arabia

stocktake_row.File: Hossain et al. - 2003 - Remote Sensing and GIS Applications for Suitable Mangrove Afforestation Area Selection in the Coasta.pdf
stocktake_row.Input_Variables: Soil texture (Soil Resources Development Institute, Bangladesh); Tidal area (Landsat TM image 12 February 1999); Soil pH (Soil Resources Development Institute, Bangladesh); Soil salinity (Soil Resources Development Institute, Bangladesh); Existing land use patterns (field investigations; government offices and local people)
stocktake_row.Spatial_Method: ISODATA unsupervised classification; Maximum Likelihood supervised classification; weighted and scored land suitability assessment (three classes: most suitable, moderately suitable, not suitable) based on soil type, soil pH, soil salinity, tidal area and existing land use to identify suitable mangrove afforestation areas.
stocktake_row.Tool_Source: ENVI : Used as the image processing software to analyze Landsat TM imagery and perform both unsupervised (ISODATA) and supervised (ROI-based, parallelepiped and Maximum Likelihood) classifications to derive the land-use/land-suitability map for mangrove afforestation.
stocktake_row.Output: Land suitability map for mangrove afforestation [Most suitable; Moderately suitable; Not suitable]
stocktake_row.Geographic_Scope: Sub-national: Cox's Bazar district; National: Bangladesh
stocktake_row.Narrative: The study addressed mangrove afforestation along Cox’s Bazar coast as a Nature-based Solution to mitigate cyclones. Inputs included Landsat TM imagery (12 Feb 1999) to locate mudflats; 1:10,000 topographic maps (Survey of Bangladesh, 1999); 1:50,000 soil maps (Soil Resources Development Institute, 1996/1999); a digitized study-area map; and field data from 50 plots. A GIS-based land-suitability assessment weighted five criteria (soil texture 30, tidal area 30, soil pH 10, soil salinity 10, land use 20) and scored three levels (3/2/1), with Maximum Likelihood classification. Ground truth from 50 plots yielded RMS error 0.49, less than one 30 m pixel. Outputs included a land-suitability map at ~30 m resolution, classifying areas as most suitable (2,146 ha), moderately suitable (1,605 ha) and not suitable (1,524 ha). Geographic scope was Cox’s Bazar district, southeastern Bangladesh (lat 21°15'–22°N, lon 91°45'–92°15'E). Cyclone protection motivated the study; climate risk and economic factors were not explicit inputs.
stocktake_row.Scalability_A_Justification: The analysis was applied to the Cox’s Bazar district coastal zone in Bangladesh, identifying suitable mangrove afforestation areas within that district; this represents a sub-national (local) application at district scale.
stocktake_row.Scalability_B_Justification: The method relies on a standard GIS-based weighted overlay for land suitability (with a classification and Multi-Criteria Decision Analysis approach), but the weights and criteria are tailored to Cox’s Bazar’s mangrove context, so applying it elsewhere would require re-weighting and local parameter tuning
stocktake_row.Scalability_C_Justification: Reasoning: The study mainly relies on Bangladesh-specific geospatial layers—1) Landsat TM imagery (global and openly available) but 2) topographic maps at 1:10,000, soil maps at 1:50,000 from SRDI, a locally digitized base map, and local field/training data, plus local tidal records (BIWTA); these national-scale inputs would need to be substituted with equivalents in another region, limiting generalizability.
stocktake_row.oa_title: Remote Sensing and GIS Applications for Suitable Mangrove Afforestation Area Selection in the Coastal Zone of Bangladesh

stocktake_row.File: Jusoff - 2008 - Geospatial Information Technology for Conservation of Coastal Forest and Mangroves Environment in Ma.pdf
stocktake_row.Input_Variables: Soil Fertility (ECOCROP database); Drainage (ECOCROP database); Texture (ECOCROP database); Depth (ECOCROP database); pH (ECOCROP database); Slope (Topography map); Cloud Cover (Satellite imagery); Snow Cover (Satellite imagery); Soil Moisture (Satellite imagery); Topography (Topography map); Basin Boundary (Geographical boundary map); Road Network (Ways network); Land Use/Land Cover (Land use/land cover map)
stocktake_row.Spatial_Method: Boolean method-based site suitability analysis; Fuzzy method-based site suitability analysis; GIS-based overlay and multiplication of environmental factor maps to identify suitable mangrove planting areas and to express degrees of suitability via fuzzy memberships.
stocktake_row.Tool_Source: IDRISI for Windows (Clark Labs) : Used as the GIS/RS software to implement fuzzy and Boolean site suitability analyses for mangrove reforestation; it provides fuzzy membership functions (Sigmoidal, J-Shaped, Linear and User-defined) and enables layering, overlaying and multiplying thematic maps to derive suitable planting sites and compare Boolean vs fuzzy classifications.
stocktake_row.Output: Mangrove site suitability map — Boolean (suitable / unsuitable); Mangrove site suitability map — Fuzzy (continuous suitability 0–1 / classes poor–high); Proposed forest land‑use allocation map (proposed forest land use plan)
stocktake_row.Climate_Benefit: Yes: They explicitly map drought severity and flood vulnerability (with historical events) to create hazard-priority zones, then spatially target rainwater harvesting as an adaptation to water scarcity and to reduce runoff-driven flood risk, demonstrated by using these hazard maps to rank wards and prioritizing high-flood areas (e.g., Oesapa) for RWHS deployment.
stocktake_row.Narrative: NbS addressed mangrove reforestation and coastal forest management in Malaysia, focusing on sustainable site selection for mangrove planting. Key inputs included GIS/RS layers (topography, basin boundary, road network) and ecological factors (soil fertility, drainage, texture, depth, pH), dynamic RS variables (cloud cover, soil moisture), FAO ECOCROP data, stakeholder interviews, and historical land-use/land-cover maps for 1973, 1987, 1993 and 1998. The approach combined two spatial methods: Boolean (0/1) and fuzzy (0–1) logic. Overlay of factor maps followed by multiplication with limitation maps produced suitable-site outputs; in the fuzzy method, membership functions (Sigmoidal, Linear, asymmetrical second degree, S) and a minimum operator were used. Validation comprised a Boolean–fuzzy comparison (Figure 6) with no field validation reported; major outputs were maps of suitable mangrove sites, land-use/land-cover maps, changes between 1987–1993 and 1993–1998, and a proposed forest land-use plan. Scope: Malaysia’s coastal mangroves; economic factors were considered; climate risk not explicitly modeled.
stocktake_row.Scalability_A_Justification: Reasoning: The study demonstrates site suitability and land-use planning for mangroves across Malaysia’s coastal/mangrove region, i.e., a country-scale application rather than a single site, indicating national-scale scope; thus, 2.
stocktake_row.Scalability_B_Justification: The method uses a general GIS-based Boolean/fuzzy suitability framework with standard overlay operations, which could be applied elsewhere, but region-specific factors, thresholds, and membership functions would need local calibration
stocktake_row.Scalability_C_Justification: The study explicitly cites the FAO ECOCROP database for quantitative soil and environmental parameters, plus mentions field measurements and local land-use/land-cover data (and remote sensing/GIS integration) in Malaysia. This combination is mixed—global, open-access inputs complemented by essential local data—so the approach is replicable in other regions using the same open datasets plus region-specific local data
stocktake_row.oa_title: Geospatial Information Technology for Conservation of Coastal Forest and Mangroves Environment in Malaysia
